title: Knowing your price
hookLine: Agrippinus kept his character though it cost him; each person knows their own price (Discourses 1.2)

cards: Agrippinus is being tried before the Senate in Rome. A messenger runs to tell him. Agrippinus says: good luck to it.
But it's the hour for exercise and a cold bath. Let's go. Later the messenger comes back.
You've been condemned. To exile, or to death? Exile.
And my property? Not taken. Then let's go out to Aricia and have lunch.

teach.b: The second discourse is titled, roughly, how to keep your own character in everything. The Greek word for character there is prosōpon, the mask and role from the handbook.
Epictetus imagines someone asking whether to hold the chamber pot for another man. If he refuses, he'll be beaten and go without food.
For a different person, it would be unbearable not only to hold it, but even to let someone else hold it for him.
If you ask me, Epictetus says, I'll tell you food is worth more than hunger and a beating is worse than none, so if that's how you measure, go and hold it. But it's beneath me?
That, he says, is something you bring to the question, not me.

teach.h: YOU KNOW AT WHAT PRICE YOU SELL YOURSELF.
teach.b: You know what you're worth to yourself, and at what price you sell yourself. People sell themselves at different prices. Then Agrippinus.
A man named Florus was weighing whether to take part in one of Nero's spectacles, appearing on stage to please the emperor. He asked Agrippinus, who said: go. Then why won't you?

teach.h: I DON'T EVEN CONSIDER THE QUESTION.
teach.b: Because, said Agrippinus, I don't even consider the question.
Once you start weighing such things, Epictetus says, setting the value of outside things against each other, you're close to those who've forgotten their own character.
Agrippinus didn't win the argument about Nero's stage. He never let it become an argument.
Knowing your price isn't pride. It's knowing, before the offer arrives, the few things that simply aren't for sale.

how: People practicing Stoicism sometimes decide in advance on a few things they will not do for any reward, so that when the offer comes they don't have to deliberate.

o: the emperor who wanted senators on his stage
the man who wouldn't even consider some questions
a senator who sold his vote to the highest bidder

games.q: I know my price — tap the pairs.
p: let's go to Aricia for lunch

s: Agrippinus told Florus not to go on Nero's stage
he told Florus to go. he himself wouldn't even consider the question.
Epictetus says everyone sells themselves at the same price
people sell themselves at different prices. you know your own.
condemned to exile, Agrippinus suggested lunch at Aricia
his property wasn't taken, so: let's go to Aricia and eat.

games.q: Florus asks Agrippinus whether to appear in Nero's spectacle. what does Agrippinus say?
o: go. but I won't, because I don't even consider the question.
go, and I'll come with you.
games.why: he tells Florus to go. for himself, the question isn't even on the table. weighing it, Epictetus says, is the first step to forgetting your character.

practice: Ask yourself quietly what you wouldn't do, even if it paid well, even if everyone else was doing it: laughing at a cruel joke to fit in, shading the truth for a sale, flattering someone to get ahead.
Find one, and picture the moment it's offered. Then picture yourself not even weighing it, just a plain no.

wordCard.voice: Agrippinus. The man who wouldn't even consider some questions; you know at what price you sell yourself. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: character, role, mask. Discourses 1.2 is about keeping it in everything.

carryVoice: Your line: I know my price. Some questions never need weighing at all, not even once. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.1.28–32 (Agrippinus' trial and lunch at Aricia)
